title: Polenta Concia
subtitle: Valdaostana polenta with butter and melted local cheese
excerpt: Polenta concia is a rich Alpine preparation from the Aosta Valley: soft polenta finished with a generous amount of butter and fontina cheese until the whole thing is one smooth, glossy mass. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Polenta concia (also spelled polenta cuncèa in Valdaostano dialect) is a dish of the Aosta Valley and the northern alpine regions of Piedmont and Lombardy, where corn polenta and the local Fontina DOP cheese have been produced side by side since at least the 17th century. Concia means 'dressed' or 'seasoned' in northern Italian dialects: the polenta is 'dressed' with fat and melted cheese to enrich it. Fernanda Gosetti, La cucina regionale italiana (1967, Mondadori), includes polenta concia as one of the definitive dishes of the Valle d'Aosta.

glossaryTerms.definition: A semi-soft cow's milk cheese from the Aosta Valley with a mild, nutty flavour and exceptional melting properties. It is the cheese required for polenta concia and for fondue valdostana. Substitutes: Gruyère, Comté, or Emmental, all of which melt similarly.

content.text: Polenta concia is the most fortifying of Alpine dishes. Soft polenta is cooked until thick, then stirred with cold butter and Fontina until the cheese melts completely into the polenta and the whole thing becomes a smooth, yielding, intensely rich dish. It is winter food: filling, warming, and utterly simple.

Use instant polenta for a 5-minute version or traditional coarse polenta for a 40-minute one; both produce good results. The Fontina must melt, so cut it into small pieces and add gradually. The finished dish should be soft enough to serve from a spoon: if it sets firm, stir in a little more hot water.

Bring {{water}} of water (or water and milk combined) to the boil in a large heavy-based saucepan. Add {{salt-table}} of salt. Whisk in {{polenta-coarse}} of polenta in a steady stream, whisking constantly to prevent lumps.

Reduce heat to low. Cook the polenta, stirring frequently with a wooden spoon or whisk, for the time stated on the packet: 5 minutes for instant, 35 to 40 minutes for traditional coarse polenta. It should pull away from the sides of the pan and be thick and smooth.

Remove from the heat. Stir in {{unsalted-butter}} of cold butter piece by piece until melted. Add {{fontina}} of diced Fontina a handful at a time, stirring after each addition until the cheese melts completely. Add Parmesan if using.

Season with {{black-pepper}} of black pepper. Taste for salt. If the polenta has tightened, stir in a little hot water to loosen it to a soft, spoonable consistency. Serve immediately in warm shallow bowls.

items.cause: Polenta added too quickly to the water, or water not boiling when it was added
items.fix: Add polenta in a slow, thin stream while whisking constantly. Lumps can sometimes be beaten out; if not, pass through a sieve or blend.

items.symptom: Cheese forms stringy clumps rather than melting smoothly
items.cause: Polenta temperature too low, or cheese added all at once
items.fix: The polenta must be off the heat but still very hot when the cheese goes in. Add in small batches and stir vigorously between additions.

items.symptom: Polenta sets too firm before serving
items.cause: Polenta cooled too much, or water ratio too low
items.fix: Return to low heat with a splash of water or milk and stir until loosened.

content.text: Polenta concia comes from the Aosta Valley, Italy's smallest region, wedged between Switzerland and France in the western Alps. It is mountain food in every sense: calorie-dense, warming, made from the two things the valley produces in abundance, corn and alpine milk.

is one of Italy's most important cheeses, with protected designation of origin from the Aosta Valley, and polenta concia is the dish that shows it to best effect. It is served on its own as a first course, or alongside braised meats and game.
